author.name: Debra Hawhee
author.affiliation_at_time: Pennsylvania State University (Department of English; Rhetoric / Communication Arts)

essay_title: Looking Into Aristotle's Eyes: Toward a Theory of Rhetorical Vision
publication: Advances in the History of Rhetoric 14.2 (2011): 139-165

section_structure.title: (Untitled introduction)
section_structure.summary: Oedipus + DA 428a.15-16 epigraphs; programmatic claim that rhetorical vision unifies the three books of the Rhetoric and bridges it to DA / Parva Naturalia.

section_structure.title: PHANTASIA AND RHETORIC
section_structure.summary: Survey of the scholarship on phantasia (Schofield, Watson, Caston, Modrak, Nussbaum, O'Gorman, Frede, Kennerly); positions phantasia as fuzzy, distance- and remove-related visual faculty.

section_structure.title: PHANTASIA AND THE RHETORIC
section_structure.summary: Reads Rhet. I.11 (1370a.28-29) 'phantasia is a kind of weak perception' in context of pleasure, desire, judicial argument; introduces deliberative phantasia (phantasia bouleutikē) from DA 3.11; treats hyperochē, auxēsis, megethos in Book I.9/14.

section_structure.title: DISPOSITIONAL VISION: PHANTASIA AND THE PATHĒ
section_structure.summary: Book II as the site where phantasia and pathē interpenetrate; anger (2.2.1378a.30-32), shame (2.6.1384a.21-24, 1384a.33-35), and the phainesthai/phaineinroot are pressed; explicit citation of Nussbaum 1985 p.265 and p.264 (deliberative phantasia).

section_structure.title: RHETORICAL VISION THROUGH LEXIS
section_structure.summary: Book III (chs. 2, 10, 11) on metaphor, urbanity (asteia), pro ommatōn poiein (3.10.1410b.33-35), energeia (3.11.1411b.22-23 ff.); Moran 1996 on Burke's 'setting before the eyes'.

section_structure.title: RHETORICAL VISION IN DEMOSTHENES' EPITAPHIOS
section_structure.summary: Case study of the 338 BCE funeral oration after Chaironeia; Loraux and Derderian on epitaphios; Demosthenes' phaos/light metaphor, footprint metaphor, density of phantasiai overtaking the corpses.

section_structure.title: CONCLUSION
section_structure.summary: Theoretical upshot — words facilitate vision, drive deliberative phantasia, bridge to contemporary neuroscience (Kosslyn & Thompson 2003) on visual cortex activation by language.

outline: Hawhee opens (p.139) by juxtaposing two epigraphs — Oedipus's promise to the Stranger that 'in everything I say there will be vision' (OC l.74) and Aristotle's DA 428a.15-16 — to make her programmatic claim: words can stand in for and facilitate vision (horōnta). She announces that rhetorical vision, a 'cluster of terms that bears on [Aristotle's] theory of visual style' (p.139), unifies the Rhetoric's three books and ties it to DA and the Parva Naturalia (p.140). The thesis is that phantasia is the central faculty for rhetorical vision: a fuzzy, distance-related, judgment-feeding capacity by which images can be both conjured and communicated (pp.140-141, 144). She distinguishes 'rhetorical vision' from 'visual rhetoric' (Finnegan, Blakesley & Brooke): visual rhetoric studies the rhetorical work of pictorial objects, while rhetorical vision studies how words form perception (p.140). She rejects the merely metaphorical reading of 'seeing-as-understanding' (p.141, contra Kennedy 2007), insisting that phantasia operates 'at the level of direct sensory perception' as well as in cognition. The first section, 'Phantasia and Rhetoric' (pp.141-144), surveys scholarship: Schofield 1992, Watson 1982, Caston 1996, Modrak 1986, Nussbaum 1985, Frede 1992, O'Gorman 2005, Kennerly 2010; Aristotle's etymology of phantasia from phaos (DA 429a.4-5); the bronze-mirror and 'man-in-the-distance' examples (DA passim) as paradigms of phantasia's 'fuzziness.' The second section, 'Phantasia and the Rhetoric' (pp.144-149), centers on Rhet. I.11.1370a.28-29 ('phantasia is a kind of weak perception'), reading it in context of pleasure, desire, motive, and judicial invention; she introduces deliberative phantasia (phantasia bouleutikē) from DA 3.11.434a.6-11 and DA 3.7.431b.6-8; she traces phantasia through Book I.9 (hyperochē, auxēsis), I.12 (witnesses, babies and animals), I.14 (heaping of wrongs, 1.14.1375a.8-11), and shows that 'the more images that can be gathered under one's honor, the better' (paraphrasing 1.9.1368a-1371a). The third section, 'Dispositional Vision: Phantasia and the Pathē' (pp.149-152), traverses Book II: anger (2.2.1378a.30-32) defined via phainomenēs/n; shame (2.6.1384a.21-24, 1384a.33-35) as 'phantasia about loss of reputation'; the verb phainein and its forms (phainesthai, phaineinetai, ophthalmois). On p.152 Hawhee explicitly cites Nussbaum 1985: 'in book II, phantasia moves closer to the way Nussbaum (1985) figures it — as interpretation, but it is interpretation that is grafted onto direct perception: rhetorical vision depends upon both simultaneously.' The fourth section, 'Rhetorical Vision through Lexis' (pp.152-155), reads Rhet. III: Licymnius and beautiful words (3.2.1405b.5-7); Bryson's substitutability thesis refuted by 'making the thing appear before the eyes' (3.2 ff.); urbanity / asteia (3.10) and the canonical pro ommatōn poiein definition at 3.10.1410b.33-35; energeia defined at 3.11.1411b.22-23 ('I call those things before-the-eyes that signify things engaged in activity') and elaborated 3.11.1411b.26-32, 1411b.33-1412a.5; Aristotle's link of energeia to motion/life at 3.11.1412a.9-10; metaphysical anchor Metaph. 9.5.1048a.32-34 ('Energeia means the presence of the thing'); Moran 1996 and Burke's 'setting before the eyes' (Rhetoric of Motives 1950/1969, 86-87). The fifth section, 'Rhetorical Vision in Demosthenes' Epitaphios' (pp.155-159), reads the 338 BCE oration after Chaironeia; engages Loraux 2006, Derderian 2001; centers Demosthenes' light/phaos analogy (Funeral Speech 24), the 'thronging' (prosistamena/panta) of memories (15), Demosthenes' use of 'making visible' (dēloun, 13), and the footprint metaphor (16) — all read as performative tappings of phantasia. The conclusion (pp.159-160) argues that words have the capacity to bring energetic images before the eyes, to compete with or overtake what is already before the audience's eyes, leading audiences into deliberative phantasia and thus belief-formation; she bridges to contemporary neuroscience (Kosslyn & Thompson 2003 on visual-cortex activation by language; Prasad, Thomas, & Aguirre 2008 on the congenitally blind). The 28 notes (pp.160-162) extend the argument to Quintilian, Vico, Priestley, Burke, and to medieval mnemonics via Carruthers 2008.

concepts.label: rhetorical vision
concepts.definition: Hawhee's signature construct: the capacity by which words form, conjure, or alter visual perception in audiences; a theory abstracted from a 'cluster of terms' in Aristotle's Rhetoric (phantasia, pro ommatōn poiein, energeia, enargeia, megethos, hyperochē, asteia). Distinguished from 'visual rhetoric' (which studies pictorial objects) by its focus on language-as-vision-producer (pp.139-141).

concepts.label: phantasia (faculty)
concepts.definition: For Hawhee, the central rhetorical faculty: a 'fuzzy' visual capacity that operates when vision happens at some remove (memory, distance, dreams, mirrors); the dynamic of conjuring images for judgment, desire, and pathos (pp.140, 142-143).

concepts.label: pro ommatōn poiein (bringing-before-the-eyes)
concepts.definition: Aristotle's stylistic strategy (Rhet. 3.10-11) for making things appear; for Hawhee the principal lexical engine of rhetorical vision, gathering future and past images into 'the now' as lively, vivid, kinetic (p.153).

concepts.label: energeia (rhetorical activity / actuality)
concepts.definition: From Rhet. 3.11.1411b.22-23 and Metaph. 9.5.1048a.32-34: 'presence of the thing'; in style, the depiction of subjects as engaged in activity, motion, life (kinēsis, zōos), which 'pours words as lively images into the eyes' (p.154).

concepts.label: enargeia (vividness)
concepts.definition: Visual-stylistic vividness; Hawhee glosses Kennedy's translation of energeia/enargeia as 'visual-rhetorical concepts' (p.140); she keeps the pair in productive tension across the article.

concepts.label: deliberative phantasia (phantasia bouleutikē)
concepts.definition: From DA 3.11.434a.6-11 and 3.7.431b.6-8: the calculative combination of several images into one (pleionōn phantasmatōn) so that a single composite picture grounds decision; for Hawhee, the faculty that lets rhetors heap, amplify, and let audiences invent alongside (pp.148, 155).

concepts.label: phantasia-pathos integration
concepts.definition: Hawhee's thesis (p.151): 'phantasia and pathē could not exist outside a matrix of phantastic visibility'; pathē are seen through phantasia (anger, shame, fear, pleasure), and phantasia is grafted onto direct perception (p.152).

concepts.label: phantasia as weak perception
concepts.definition: Rhet. I.11.1370a.28-29 (phantasia estin aisthēsis tis asthenēs); Hawhee insists this line cannot be read in isolation as oracular essence but must be situated in the pleasure-and-desire context of Book I.11 (pp.144-145).

concepts.label: fuzziness / distance-dependence of phantasia
concepts.definition: Hawhee's leading characterization (p.143): bronze mirrors, distant figures, after-images, dreams all share a 'kind of fuzziness'; phantasia 'enters the picture when vision happens at some remove.'

concepts.label: phainein verbal cluster
concepts.definition: Forms of phainein (phainesthai, phaineinetai, phainomenēs, phantasiai, phantasmata) populate Book II.1-2's definitions of anger and the apparent (p.150).

concepts.label: hyperochē (superiority / heaping)
concepts.definition: Read by Hawhee (Note 20) as a rhetorical strategy that combines superiority with density of images — 'piling on excessive details' (1.14.1375a.8-11; 1.9.1368a.23, .27) — and so a near-visual amplifier complementary to phantasia (pp.147-149).

concepts.label: auxēsis (amplification)
concepts.definition: 1.9.1368a.25-30, 1.9.1368a.40-1368a.27: amplification 'aims to show hyperochē'; for Hawhee a rhetorical companion to deliberative phantasia (pp.148-149).

concepts.label: megethos (greatness / magnitude)
concepts.definition: 1.9.1368a.25-30: epideictic 'clothes' actions with greatness and beauty; loftiness invoking measures, stellar magnitudes (p.149).

concepts.label: asteia (urbanity / urbane wit)
concepts.definition: Rhet. 3.10: stylistic vividness, achieved through pro ommatōn poiein; the chapter Hawhee uses as the proof text for words rendering futures and pasts as present (pp.152-153).

concepts.label: metaphora (metaphor)
concepts.definition: Rhet. 3.2 and 3.10-11: the metaphor that 'sets before the eyes' is one whose terms signify activity (energeia); for Hawhee the most concentrated locus of rhetorical vision (pp.152-154).

concepts.label: kinēsis / zōos (movement / life)
concepts.definition: Rhet. 3.11.1412a.9-10: 'He makes everything move and live, and energeia is motion'; the kinetic-vivific signature of rhetorical vision (p.154).

concepts.label: phaos (light) etymology
concepts.definition: DA 3.3.429a.4-5: Aristotle's 'somewhat dubious' etymology of phantasia from phaos (light); for Hawhee a key bridge to Demosthenes' light/dark imagery (pp.142, 157).

concepts.label: shame as phantasia of reputation loss
concepts.definition: Rhet. 2.6.1384a.21-24: shame as phantasia about loss of reputation; 'shame is in the eyes' (proverb); shame as 'irreducibly social' (Gross 2006) and irreducibly visual (p.151).

concepts.label: anger as phainomenēs slight
concepts.definition: Rhet. 2.2.1378a.30-32: anger requires that the slight and desired retaliation appear (phainomenēs/n) as such; perception-as-interpretation in Nussbaum's sense (p.150).

concepts.label: throng / density of images
concepts.definition: Demosthenes (Funeral Speech 15) 'throngs' (prosistamena/panta); Hawhee's term for a cumulative density of phantasiai that overtakes the corpses before the audience's eyes (pp.157-159).

concepts.label: footprint metaphor (Demosthenes 16)
concepts.definition: Memory as visually locating imprints left by activities of the dead; for Hawhee a 'bringing-before-the-eyes' loaded with implied energeia (pp.158-159).

concepts.label: rhetorical vision is not merely metaphorical 'seeing-as'
concepts.definition: Programmatic distinction (p.141): rhetorical vision occurs near or at the level of direct sensory perception, not only at the level of cognitive metaphor (contra Kennedy 2007, 222).

concepts.label: rhetorical vision vs. visual rhetoric
concepts.definition: Visual rhetoric (Finnegan, Blakesley/Brooke, Hariman/Lucaites, Kimble) studies plastic, photographic, televisual artifacts; rhetorical vision considers how words form perception (p.140).

concepts.label: communicative synesthesia
concepts.definition: Hawhee's phrase (p.140) for the Poetics-Rhetoric overlap: arts that 'tap into bodily and visual faculties' through words.

concepts.label: composite image (Wolfson 1935)
concepts.definition: Phantasia bouleutikē as Wolfson's 'compositive sort of imagination' (1935, 92) — the layered image that bundles multiple principles (p.148; cf. Moran/Burke pp.154-155).

concepts.label: neural-imagery bridge
concepts.definition: Hawhee's closing move (pp.159-160): Kosslyn & Thompson 2003 on visual-cortex activation by mental imagery and language; Prasad, Thomas, & Aguirre 2008 on congenitally-blind cross-modal processing — situates Aristotle as anticipatory rather than antique.

concepts.label: saying heightens the seeing
concepts.definition: Hawhee's recurring formula (pp.147, 151, 160): the act of vouching, broadcasting, narrating, or eulogizing intensifies and 'spreads' phantastic images.

readings.thesis: Rhetorical vision lends unity to the Rhetoric's famously various three books, threading pleasure/desire in Book I, pathē in Book II, and lexis (pro ommatōn poiein, energeia) in Book III (p.140).

Phantasia in the Rhetoric operates not only on the level of cognitive metaphor ('seeing-as-understanding') but at or near the level of direct sensory perception; rhetors mobilize visual capacity itself, not just understanding (pp.141, 144, 154).

Hawhee positions her reading 'between' the imagist scholars (Modrak) and the interpretivist (Nussbaum 1985): in Book II 'phantasia moves closer to the way Nussbaum (1985) figures it — as interpretation, but it is interpretation that is grafted onto direct perception' (p.152).

Deliberative phantasia (DA 3.11.434a) — the heaping of phantasmata into one composite — relocates invention from the rhetor alone to the audience, since hearers must engage imaginatively with the bundle of principles each image contains (pp.155, 159).

Demosthenes' Epitaphios (338 BCE) performatively enacts Aristotelian rhetorical vision: light/phaos analogy, throng of memories, footprint metaphor, and 'making visible' (dēloun) overtake the visible corpses with phantasiai (pp.155-159).

Aristotle's account of phantasia is not 'an archaic relic' but a 'provocative set of observations' consonant with contemporary neuroscience on visual-cortex activation by language and mental imagery (pp.159-160).

greek_terms.gloss: Visual faculty; for Hawhee a fuzzy, distance-related, judgment-feeding capacity; not aisthēsis; central faculty for rhetorical vision.
Image presented by phantasia; the 'pleionōn phantasmatōn' of DA 3.11 are combined in deliberative phantasia.
Plural; Quintilian's visiones; voice as 'sound with phantasiai' (DA 2.8.420b.29-33).
'To show, disclose, bring to light, appear'; the verbal root of phantasia; saturates Rhet. II.1-2 (anger definition).
'To phantasize' — Hawhee's English coinage from the verbal form.
Deliberative phantasia (DA 3.11.434a.6-11); calculative combination of multiple images into one composite for judgment.
Light; the (dubious) etymological root Aristotle gives for phantasia at DA 429a.4-5; Demosthenes' light/dark imagery (Funeral Speech 24).
'Bringing-before-the-eyes' (Rhet. 3.10.1410b.33-35; 3.11.1411b.22-23) — the stylistic operation that signifies things engaged in activity.
'Placing before the eyes' — Poetics 17.1.1455a — Sophoclean dramatic technique transferred to verbal art.
Activity, actuality; in style, 'signify things engaged in activity' (Rhet. 3.11.1411b.22-23); 'presence of the thing' (Metaph. 9.5.1048a.32-34); opposed to dunamis.
Vividness; paired with energeia by Kennedy as 'visual-rhetorical concepts' (p.140).
Sensation, direct perception; phantasia distinct from aisthēsis (DA 428a.5-8); paired with phantasia in 'weak perception' phrase.
Dative of aisthēsis used in Rhet. 3.11 metaphor passage — 'visualization (opsei) or some other sense perception (aisthēsei).'
'Sensory' (DA 3.11.434a.6) — 'phantasia in the form of sense.'
Style, diction; the matter of Rhet. III; the medium through which rhetors tap phantasia.
Emotion(s); 'seen through phantasia' (p.150); 'irreducibly visual' (Hawhee on Gross 2006).
Speaker's character; 'sutured to rhetoric' via reputation that 'heightens the seeing' (p.147).
Metaphor; in Rhet. 3.2 and 3.10-11 the chief carrier of energeia and bringing-before-the-eyes.
Urbanity, wit (Rhet. 3.10); achieved by pro ommatōn poiein.
Amplification; aims to show hyperochē (1.9.1368a.40); home in epideictic; Hawhee links to Isocrates' auxein.
Superiority / heaping; 'piling on' of active images (1.14.1375a.8-11); for Hawhee a bridge to phantasia's density.
Prefix 'excessive/above' + 'support/prop'; etymological pressure Hawhee applies (p.148).
Magnitude, greatness, loftiness (1.9.1368a.25-30); epideictic's task to clothe actions in megethos.
Movement; 'energeia is motion' (Rhet. 3.11.1412a.9-10); Kennerly's 'rhetorical kinesis.'
Living; paired with kinēsis as the vivific dimension of energeia.
Picture (De Memoria); pressed-in 'kind of picture' on the soul (1.450a.27ff.).
'To see (in physical sense)' — present participle invoked by Oedipus and parsed at p.139.
Visualization, sight; 3.11.1411b.34-1412a.5 'visualization or some other form of sense perception'; Stanford 1936 on 'opsis in words.'
'In the eyes' — Rhet. 2.6.1384a.34 in proverb 'shame is in the eyes.'
'To make clear / visible' — Demosthenes Funeral Speech 13 ('making visible the deeds of these men').
'To see and possess' — Rhet. 1.11.1370a.25-27; locates desire in visual longing.
'Apparent pleasures' — the rhetorically operative class of pleasures (Rhet. 1.11).
'Apparent / conspicuous' (Rhet. 2.2.1378a.31) — Kennedy's 'conspicuous'; Harris 1997 on the philological case.
'Broadcasters / proclaimers' (Rhet. 2.6.6); 'ex-' + 'tell out'; Hawhee distinguishes from mere aggeltikous.
'To many' (Rhet. 2.6.6) — broadcasting shame to many.
'Calculative' (DA 3.11.434a.7) — the calculative part where deliberative phantasia operates.
'Multiple images' (DA 3.11.434a.10) — the bouleutic combination.
'Meaning-making' (DA 2.8.420b.32) — voice's distinguishing capacity, tied to phantasia.
'Noise / sound' — opposed to phōnē + phantasia in DA 2.8.420b.29-33.
'Being disposed' (Rhet. 2.1.1377b-1378a) — layered hexeis / dispositional vision.
'A certain emotion' (Rhet. 1.11.1370a.31) — pathos at the seat of pleasure-perception.
'At one and the same time' / 'on this one occasion' (Demosthenes Funeral Speech 15) — kairos invaded by phantasia.
'Hard to grasp and fierce' (Demosthenes Funeral Speech 24) — the post-light condition.
'Coming into / all' (Demosthenes Funeral Speech 15) — translator's 'thronging.'
'Symbolic monument' (Loraux 2006, 121) — funeral oration as taphos.

tensions.label: Imagist vs. interpretivist phantasia
tensions.description: Modrak/Watson (image-recall) vs. Nussbaum 1985 (interpretation, 'abstract thought thought to concrete perceptibles'); Hawhee mediates — Book II's phantasia 'moves closer to Nussbaum' but is 'grafted onto direct perception' (p.152). Caston 1996 (Note 12) follows Nussbaum's logic linking phantasia to Plato; most others, Hawhee notes, foreground images rather strenuously.

tensions.label: Metaphorical vs. non-metaphorical 'seeing'
tensions.description: Kennedy (2007, 222) uses scare quotes around 'bringing-before-the-eyes' to imply 'seeing-as-understanding'; Hawhee argues (Notes 15, 25) that rhetorical vision occurs 'near or at the level of direct sensory perception,' a non-metaphorical reading. Newman 2002 partially shares this with respect to metaphor specifically.

tensions.label: Unity vs. heterogeneity of the Rhetoric
tensions.description: Gross & Dascal 2001, McAdon 2004, Poster 1997, Ross 1995, Barnes 1995 debate the unity of the Rhetoric (Note 6); Hawhee adds rhetorical vision as a new unity-thread, threading I (pleasure/desire/honor), II (pathē), III (lexis).

tensions.label: Material corpses vs. phantastic words (Demosthenes)
tensions.description: Loraux 2006: epitaphios as 'imaginary without image,' an effacement of sensory vision; Derderian 2001: epitaphios overrides the inscribed monument by abstraction. Hawhee inverts: the speech does not abstract — it overtakes the material visible with denser, kinetic phantasiai (pp.156-159).

tensions.label: Visual rhetoric (object-centered) vs. rhetorical vision (word-centered)
tensions.description: Finnegan, Hariman/Lucaites, Kimble, Blakesley/Brooke center pictorial artifacts; Hawhee insists on the complementary, language-driven side. Finnegan's 2008 'twofold' definition is salvaged as compatible (p.140).

tensions.label: Eye vs. ear in stylistics
tensions.description: Note 7: 'similar theoretical work has been done with a focus on sound' (Porter 2004, Graff 2001); Hawhee privileges the eye but acknowledges parallel work on audition.

cross_pipeline_bridges.bridge: Hawhee's Rhetoric I/II/III + DA + Poet. + Metaph. + De Memoria + De Motu Animalium constitute a near-complete Aristotelian phantasia map — Bekker loci above feed the Aristotelian KU map directly.

Daniel Gross 2006 (Secret History of Emotion) is cited at p.151 — Hawhee's reading of shame as 'irreducibly social and irreducibly visual' is direct bridge to the Rhetorical Ontology pipeline's situated-emotion thesis.
Konstan 2007's 'classical view of pathē as arising in and from social interactions' (Note 22) + Aristotle Rhet. 2.6 shame analysis = canonical bridge to the situated-emotion subcluster.
Burke Rhetoric of Motives (1950/1969, 86-87) quoted via Moran 1996 — sets up Hawhee's monograph trajectory.
Kosslyn & Thompson 2003; Prasad, Thomas, & Aguirre 2008; Cohen et al. 2002; Mildner 2008; Slobin 2008 — Hawhee opens a neurorhetorical extension lane.

nussbaum_comparison: Hawhee's most consequential engagement with the cluster is her explicit alignment with Nussbaum 1985 at p.152, where she writes: 'in book II, phantasia moves closer to the way Nussbaum (1985) figures it — as interpretation, but it is interpretation that is grafted onto direct perception: rhetorical vision depends upon both simultaneously.' This is at once a citation and a refinement. Nussbaum had argued, against the prevailing 'imagist' readings (Beare, Hamlyn, Schofield in part, and later Modrak), that phantasia is best understood as a generic interpretive capacity by which an animal sees an x as a y — phantasia 'ties abstract thought to concrete perceptible objects or situations' (Nussbaum 1985, 265, paraphrased at Hawhee p.142). Hawhee takes from Nussbaum: (a) the interpretive valence, especially as it lights up Rhet. 2.2's definition of anger via phainomenēs/n (the slight must appear as such); (b) the explicit defense of 'envisaging' as a component of deliberative phantasia (Nussbaum 1985, 264, paraphrased Hawhee p.148 — 'According to Nussbaum, who otherwise argues against a purely imagistic reading of phantasia, this passage suggests on the contrary some sort of envisaging'); (c) the view that phantasia traffics between the immaterial and the material. Hawhee then adds three things Nussbaum did not develop: (1) the grafting clause — interpretation does not float free of direct perception but is grafted onto it, restoring some of what the imagist tradition wanted to preserve; (2) the rhetorical-vision construct itself, which Nussbaum's De Motu-anchored analysis did not pursue because she focused on action-explanation rather than persuasion; and (3) the phaos-derived, 'fuzzy,' distance-dependent character of phantasia, which Hawhee documents from DA 429a.4-5 and the bronze-mirror passages — a feature Nussbaum's interpretivist account underplays in favor of inferential structure. The net is a critical settling: Hawhee positions herself between Modrak (imagist) and Nussbaum (interpretivist), claiming both axes for rhetoric. Note 12 also signals that Nussbaum and Caston 'would probably disagree with my wish to stress image' — a candid recognition that Hawhee's emphasis on imagery is greater than Nussbaum's. The relation is therefore one of debt + extension + mild divergence on emphasis.
